concepts.title: What is a Graph?
concepts.contentHtml:
A graph is a set of vertices (points) connected by edges (lines). That's it!

Graphs model relationships: people connected by friendships, cities connected by roads, web pages connected by links.

Key vocabulary:

• Degree of a vertex: number of edges touching it
• Path: a sequence of edges connecting two vertices
• Connected: every pair of vertices has a path between them

concepts.title: The Handshaking Lemma
concepts.contentHtml:
The Handshaking Lemma: the sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges.

Why? Each edge contributes 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints.

Consequence: the number of vertices with odd degree must be even. (Try it! You can't draw a graph where exactly 3 vertices have odd degree.)

This simple observation is surprisingly powerful for proving impossibility results.

concepts.title: Special Graphs
concepts.contentHtml:
Complete graph Kₙ: every pair of vertices is connected. K₃ is a triangle, K₄ has 6 edges, K₅ has 10.

Bipartite graph: vertices split into two groups, edges only between groups. Think of matching students to projects.

Tree: a connected graph with no cycles. n vertices, n-1 edges. Trees are the "most efficient" connected graphs.

Planar graph: can be drawn on a plane without edges crossing.

title: Eulerian & Hamiltonian Paths
description: Can you traverse every edge? Every vertex?

concepts.title: The Königsberg Bridge Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1736, Euler asked: can you walk through Königsberg crossing each bridge exactly once?

He proved it was impossible — and in doing so, invented graph theory.

An Eulerian path traverses every edge exactly once. An Eulerian circuit does so and returns to the start.

Euler's Theorem: An Eulerian circuit exists iff every vertex has even degree. An Eulerian path exists iff exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree.

concepts.title: Hamiltonian Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once. A Hamiltonian cycle does so and returns to the start.

Unlike Euler paths, there is no simple criterion for when Hamiltonian paths exist. Checking is NP-complete — one of the hardest problems in computer science!

The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP): find the shortest Hamiltonian cycle through a set of cities. It's NP-hard, and billions of dollars depend on approximate solutions (logistics, chip design, DNA sequencing).

concepts.title: Euler vs Hamilton Comparison
concepts.contentHtml:
A useful comparison:

Eulerian: Visit every edge once. Easy to check (degree condition). Polynomial-time algorithm.

Hamiltonian: Visit every vertex once. Hard to check. NP-complete.

The gap between these two similar-sounding problems is one of the great mysteries of computer science. It's closely related to the P vs NP problem — another Millennium Prize question!

title: Graph Coloring
description: How many colors do you need?

concepts.title: Vertex Coloring
concepts.contentHtml:
Graph coloring: assign colors to vertices so that no two adjacent vertices share a color.

The chromatic number χ(G) is the minimum number of colors needed.

χ(Kₙ) = n (complete graphs need one color per vertex).
χ(tree) = 2 (trees are always 2-colorable).
χ(cycle of even length) = 2, odd length = 3.

Practical use: scheduling! Courses that share students can't be at the same time — this is graph coloring.

concepts.title: The Four Color Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
The Four Color Theorem: every planar graph can be properly colored with at most 4 colors.

This means any map can be colored with 4 colors so that neighboring regions have different colors. Conjectured in 1852, proved in 1976 — the first major theorem proved by computer.

The proof checked 1,936 configurations by machine. This was controversial: can a proof no human can verify really be trusted? The debate shaped philosophy of mathematics.

concepts.title: Chromatic Polynomials
concepts.contentHtml:
The chromatic polynomial P(G, k) counts the number of proper colorings using at most k colors.

For a complete graph: P(Kₙ, k) = k(k-1)(k-2)...(k-n+1).

For a tree with n vertices: P(T, k) = k(k-1)ⁿ⁻¹.

These polynomials encode deep structural information about the graph and connect graph theory to algebra.

title: Trees, Networks, & Algorithms
description: Spanning trees, shortest paths, and real-world networks

concepts.title: Spanning Trees
concepts.contentHtml:
A spanning tree of a graph G is a tree that includes all vertices and is a subgraph of G.

Every connected graph has a spanning tree (possibly many). A minimum spanning tree (MST) minimizes total edge weight.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges by weight, greedily add the lightest edge that doesn't create a cycle.
Prim's algorithm: grow the tree one edge at a time, always choosing the cheapest connection to a new vertex.

MSTs are used in network design, clustering, and circuit wiring.

concepts.title: Shortest Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph (with non-negative weights).

It's a greedy algorithm: always extend the path to the nearest unvisited vertex.

Used by: GPS navigation, network routing, game AI pathfinding.

For graphs with negative edges, use Bellman-Ford. For all-pairs shortest paths, use Floyd-Warshall.

concepts.title: Real-World Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
Graph theory is the mathematics of networks:

Social networks: Small-world phenomenon — ~6 degrees of separation. Power-law degree distributions (few hubs, many low-degree nodes).

The internet: Routers as vertices, connections as edges. BGP routing is graph algorithms in real time.

Biology: Protein interaction networks, neural networks, food webs. Graph analysis reveals functional modules and vulnerabilities.

PageRank: Google's original algorithm models the web as a graph and ranks pages by the structure of incoming links (this connects back to eigenvalues!).

title: Network Flow
description: Max-flow, min-cut, and optimal resource allocation

concepts.title: Flow Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has a capacity (maximum amount that can pass through) and a flow (how much is currently passing through).

There is a special source vertex s (where flow originates) and a sink vertex t (where flow is consumed).

Conservation of flow: At every vertex except s and t, the total flow in equals the total flow out. Think of it like water in pipes — nothing leaks, nothing accumulates.

The value of a flow is the total amount leaving the source (or equivalently, arriving at the sink). The goal: maximize it.

concepts.title: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
A cut in a flow network is a partition of vertices into two sets S and T, with s ∈ S and t ∈ T. The capacity of the cut is the total capacity of edges crossing from S to T.

The Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem (Ford & Fulkerson, 1956): The maximum flow from s to t equals the minimum capacity of any s-t cut.

This is a profound duality: the bottleneck limiting flow is always a specific cut. Think of it as finding the weakest link in a chain of pipes. The theorem connects optimization (max flow) with structure (min cut) and has deep connections to linear programming duality.

concepts.title: Ford-Fulkerson and Applications
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm finds maximum flow by repeatedly finding augmenting paths (paths from s to t with available capacity) and pushing flow along them.

Key refinement: the Edmonds-Karp variant uses BFS to find shortest augmenting paths, guaranteeing O(VE²) time.

Applications are vast:

• Bipartite matching: Maximum matching in a bipartite graph reduces to max-flow. Used in job assignments, kidney exchange programs.
• Scheduling: Assign tasks to machines respecting capacity constraints.
• Network reliability: Min-cut tells you the fewest edges to remove to disconnect the network.
• Image segmentation: Separating foreground from background using graph cuts.

concepts.title: Adjacency and Laplacian Matrices
concepts.contentHtml:
Every graph has associated matrices that encode its structure:

The adjacency matrix A has Aᵢⱼ = 1 if vertices i and j are connected, 0 otherwise. For weighted graphs, Aᵢⱼ equals the edge weight.

The degree matrix D is diagonal with Dᵢᵢ = deg(i).

The Laplacian matrix L = D - A combines both. It's always positive semidefinite and its eigenvalues reveal deep properties of the graph.

This transforms graph theory into linear algebra — we can study combinatorial objects using continuous mathematics!
mathExpressions: L = D - A, \quad L_{ij} = \begin{cases} \deg(i) & i = j \\ -1 & (i,j) \in E \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

concepts.title: Eigenvalues and Graph Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
The eigenvalues of graph matrices encode surprising structural information:

• The smallest eigenvalue of L is always 0. Its multiplicity equals the number of connected components.
• The second-smallest eigenvalue λ₂ (the algebraic connectivity or Fiedler value) measures how well-connected the graph is. λ₂ > 0 iff the graph is connected.
• A graph is bipartite iff the spectrum of A is symmetric about 0.

Remarkably, you can often "hear the shape" of a graph from its eigenvalues alone, though non-isomorphic graphs can share the same spectrum (they're called cospectral).

concepts.title: Cheeger's Inequality and Spectral Clustering
concepts.contentHtml:
Cheeger's inequality connects the algebraic connectivity λ₂ to the combinatorial notion of the Cheeger constant h(G) (how easy it is to "cut" the graph into two balanced parts):

λ₂/2 ≤ h(G) ≤ √(2λ₂)

This bridges the continuous (eigenvalues) and discrete (cuts) perspectives.

Spectral clustering uses the eigenvectors of L to partition data into clusters. Compute the Fiedler vector (eigenvector for λ₂), then split vertices by the sign of their components. This is the foundation of modern data science techniques for community detection in social networks, image segmentation, and unsupervised learning.

concepts.title: The Erdős–Rényi Model
concepts.contentHtml:
The Erdős–Rényi model G(n, p) generates a random graph on n vertices where each possible edge is included independently with probability p.

When p is small, the graph is sparse and fragmented. When p is large, the graph is dense and connected. The magic is what happens in between.

Key results for G(n, p):
• Expected number of edges: p × C(n,2)
• Expected degree of each vertex: p(n-1)
• For constant p, the graph is almost surely connected when n is large

This model, introduced in 1959, launched the field of random graph theory and remains one of the most studied probabilistic models in mathematics.

concepts.title: Phase Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Random graphs exhibit dramatic phase transitions — sudden qualitative changes as p crosses a threshold.

The most famous: the giant component. When p < 1/n, all components are small (logarithmic in n). When p > 1/n, a single giant component emerges containing a constant fraction of all vertices.

At exactly p = 1/n, the transition is sharp — like water freezing at 0°C. Other thresholds:
• p ≈ ln(n)/n: graph becomes connected
• p ≈ ln(n)/n: every vertex has degree ≥ 1 (no isolated vertices)

These phase transitions mirror phenomena in physics (percolation theory) and explain why real networks behave the way they do.
mathExpressions: p = \frac{1}{n}: \text{ giant component emerges}, \quad p = \frac{\ln n}{n}: \text{ graph becomes connected}

concepts.title: Small-World and Scale-Free Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
Real networks (social, biological, technological) don't look like Erdős–Rényi graphs. Two important models capture what's different:

Watts-Strogatz (1998): Start with a regular lattice, then randomly rewire edges. This produces small-world networks with high clustering (your friends know each other) and short path lengths (six degrees of separation).

Barabási-Albert (1999): Grow the network by preferential attachment — new nodes connect preferentially to high-degree nodes ("the rich get richer"). This produces scale-free networks with power-law degree distributions: P(deg = k) ∼ k⁻³.

The Internet, citation networks, protein interactions, and social media all exhibit scale-free properties. These models revolutionized network science.

title: Extremal & Algebraic Graph Theory
description: Turán's theorem, Ramsey theory, and the Tutte polynomial

concepts.title: Turán's Theorem
concepts.contentHtml:
Turán's theorem (1941) answers a fundamental question: what is the maximum number of edges a graph on n vertices can have without containing a complete subgraph Kᵣ?

The answer is the Turán graph T(n, r-1): partition the vertices into r-1 groups as equally as possible and connect every pair of vertices in different groups.

For example, the maximum number of edges in a triangle-free graph (no K₃) on n vertices is ⌊n²/4⌋, achieved by the complete bipartite graph K_{⌊n/2⌋, ⌈n/2⌉}.

Turán's theorem launched extremal graph theory — the study of how local constraints (forbidden subgraphs) limit global structure (number of edges).

concepts.title: Ramsey Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Ramsey theory studies the principle that complete disorder is impossible: any sufficiently large structure must contain an ordered substructure.

The Ramsey number R(s, t) is the smallest n such that any 2-coloring of Kₙ's edges contains a red Kₛ or a blue Kₜ.

R(3, 3) = 6: Among any 6 people, there are always 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers. This can be proved elegantly by the pigeonhole principle.

Ramsey numbers grow astronomically fast. R(5, 5) is unknown but lies between 43 and 46. Erdős famously said: if aliens demanded R(5, 5), we should try to compute it; if they demanded R(6, 6), we should attack the aliens.

concepts.title: The Tutte Polynomial
concepts.contentHtml:
The Tutte polynomial T(G; x, y) is a two-variable polynomial that encodes an astonishing amount of information about a graph:

• T(G; 1, 1) = number of spanning trees
• T(G; 2, 1) = number of spanning forests
• T(G; 1, 2) = number of spanning connected subgraphs
• T(G; 2, 0) = number of acyclic orientations
• The chromatic polynomial is P(G, k) = (-1)^{|V|-c} k^c T(G; 1-k, 0)

The Tutte polynomial connects to knot theory through the Jones polynomial: certain graph invariants translate directly to knot invariants. This unexpected bridge between topology and combinatorics is one of the deepest connections in modern mathematics.
